summary:
What Was Left Behind is a narrative pixel art video game, created in Godot 4.5 for the NASA Space Apps 2026 “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge. It tells the story of the equipment humanity left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space.

The player is a Mission Control operator who, guided by radio, relives each mission with cinematics and minigames based on real events. Two missions are currently playable:

Apollo 11: the journey to the Moon, the Eagle's descent (stabilized by the rhythm of clicks), the first step, the collection of rocks, the liftoff with a force meter, and the docking.

Pioneer 10: the launch, the asteroid belt, the photos of Jupiter's moons, the solar storm, and the plaque deciphered with pulsars.

Ten other artifacts from the challenge, such as Spirit and Opportunity, Viking, Ingenuity, and Kepler, are already available on the map as locked levels.

Each completed phase awards a piece of your mission badge. Completing a mission unlocks a fact sheet with data, history, and current location of the artifact, with a link to NASA. Everything is saved in a badge notebook.

The game includes tutorials before each minigame, a pause menu with sound and help, full English and Spanish language options, and adaptive fullscreen mode.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?
What Was Left Behind is a narrative pixel-art game about the hardware humanity left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space.

  • The player is a Mission Control operator who follows radio guidance and relives each mission through cutscenes and minigames based on real events.
  • Apollo 11: the trip to the Moon, landing the Eagle by keeping it level with the rhythm of your clicks, the first step, collecting rock samples, liftoff with a power meter, and docking.
  • Pioneer 10: launch, dodging the asteroid belt, photographing Jupiter’s moons, keeping the antenna on Earth during a solar storm, and decoding the plaque’s pulsar map.
  • Ten more challenge artifacts (Spirit & Opportunity, Viking, Ingenuity, Kepler and others) already appear on the map as locked levels.
  • Each completed phase earns a piece of that mission’s badge. A finished badge unlocks a technical sheet with facts, history, the artifact’s current location and a NASA reference link, all kept in a Badge Notebook.

Benefits

  • It turns abandoned spacecraft into stories people remember.
  • Players learn through action, not reading: they don’t just read that the Eagle landed, they land it.
  • It’s free, light, bilingual and playable in short sessions, so it fits classrooms, museums and casual players.

Expected impact

  • Spark curiosity about space history and heritage, especially among students.
  • Show that “abandoned” machines still matter: the Apollo retroreflectors are still used today, and Pioneer 10 carries a message for whoever finds it.
  • The structure is data-driven, so new artifacts can be added as missions without rewriting the game.

Tools and technology

  • Engine and languages: Godot 4.5 (GL Compatibility renderer) and GDScript.
  • Content: JSON files for all texts, missions, badges and translations, plus Python scripts for data and translation work.
  • Art and sound: pixel art and visuals are drawn by code. Music and sound effects are synthesized at runtime, so the game needs no external assets.
  • Collaboration: Git and GitHub.
  • Sources: NASA NSSDCA and science.nasa.gov.
  • Hardware: standard laptops. The game runs at 640×360 scaled to any screen.
  • AI: we used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to help write code, content and media.

Creativity

  • Each minigame mirrors a real challenge: clicking rhythm for RCS thrusters, radiation spikes ruining photos, pulsar rhythms that locate the Sun on the plaque.
  • A cutscene recreates the first step, with the original quote.
  • The collectible badges assemble piece by piece and reveal the “real story” behind each artifact.

What our team considered

  • Accuracy: dates and facts are checked against NASA sources and marked for review. Gameplay values are labelled as game values, not NASA specifications.
    • Keyboard and mouse controls.
    • A tutorial card before every minigame.
    • A help guide and FAQ in the pause menu.
    • Actions that can’t fail, and retries that keep your progress.
    • Full English and Spanish.
  • Performance: a lightweight renderer for low-end computers, plus volume settings and full-screen support.
  • Tone: Mission Control narrates and the machines don’t speak, to respect the real history.
